## Guided Tutorial 11.3: Building the Monthly Measure and Saving It as a View

**Context and objective.** The controller wants one measure she can track every month: labor hours per standard hour of output, split between direct and indirect time, with the share of overtime, smoothed over a trailing twelve months. In this tutorial, you will build it as a chain of common table expressions, running and checking each step before you add the next. @fig-11-08 shows the chain you will build. You will then save it as a view in your working copy of the database, so that it can be run again with one short query.

**Prerequisites.** Complete Tutorials 11.1 and 11.2, and continue at the end of Chapter11.sql. If you start here, make the working copy as Step 1 of Tutorial 9.1 describes, and download Chapter11.sql as it stands at the end of Tutorial 11.2 from [Companion Files](#sec-companion-files). The view is saved in CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite, never in the file you downloaded. @fig-10-08 shows the labor time table that the hours step summarizes.

![The Chain of Common Table Expressions in the Monthly Measure.](/visuals/svg/fig-11-08-cte-pipeline.svg){#fig-11-08 fig-alt="A flow diagram of the view MonthlyLaborEfficiency. Two steps at the top run side by side: MonthlyOutput, which summarizes production completion lines and items into standard hours by month, up to the last day with time records, and MonthlyHours, which summarizes labor time entries into direct, indirect, and overtime hours by month. Both feed a step named Monthly, which joins them by month. Monthly feeds Trailing, which calculates the monthly ratio and the trailing twelve-month direct, indirect, and total hours per standard hour and overtime share over a named window. The final SELECT keeps the months with a full twelve-month window."}

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Build the output step and check it.** The first CTE turns the production completions into standard hours by month. Its WHERE clause counts only the output completed up to the last day with time records, as Tutorial 10.3 did, so that the last month compares hours and output over the same days.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.3: step 1, the standard hours of output by month
   WITH MonthlyOutput AS (
       SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', pc.CompletionDate) AS Month,
           SUM(pcl.QuantityCompleted * i.StandardLaborHoursPerUnit)
               AS StandardHours
       FROM ProductionCompletionLine AS pcl
           INNER JOIN ProductionCompletion AS pc
               ON pc.ProductionCompletionID = pcl.ProductionCompletionID
           INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = pcl.ItemID
       WHERE pc.CompletionDate
           <= (SELECT MAX(WorkDate) FROM LaborTimeEntry)
       GROUP BY Month
   )
   SELECT * FROM MonthlyOutput
   ORDER BY Month;
   ```

b. Read the number of rows, and the StandardHours of the first and last months.

The step returns one row for each of the 36 months, with the standard hours of the units completed. January 2024 has very little output, because it is the month in which the data begins, and December 2026 has less than a usual month, because its output stops on 11 December.

**Step 2. Build the hours step and check it.** The second CTE summarizes the manufacturing labor time by month with conditional aggregation, as Tutorial 11.1 did, but without rounding, because its sums feed later steps.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.3: step 2, the labor hours by month
   WITH MonthlyHours AS (
       SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', WorkDate) AS Month,
           SUM(CASE LaborType WHEN 'Direct Manufacturing'
               THEN RegularHours + OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END)
               AS DirectHours,
           SUM(CASE LaborType WHEN 'Indirect Manufacturing'
               THEN RegularHours + OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END)
               AS IndirectHours,
           SUM(OvertimeHours) AS OvertimeHours
       FROM LaborTimeEntry
       WHERE LaborType <> 'NonManufacturing'
       GROUP BY Month
   )
   SELECT * FROM MonthlyHours
   ORDER BY Month;
   ```

b. Read the number of rows, and the IndirectHours of March 2024.

This step also returns 36 rows. March 2024 has a row with zero indirect hours, because its direct entries create the row and the CASE passes zero, so no month is missing for a window to skip. Had the indirect hours been summarized in a step of their own, with `WHERE LaborType = 'Indirect Manufacturing'`, March 2024 would have had no row at all.

**Step 3. Join the two steps, and check the join.** The third CTE joins output and hours on the month. A check query counts its rows, because an inner join drops any month that is missing from either step.

a. Copy the query of Step 1, with its comment, to the end of the script, and change the comment to the one below.
b. Delete the copy's last two lines, type a comma after the closing parenthesis of MonthlyOutput, and paste the MonthlyHours step of Step 2 after it, from `MonthlyHours AS (` to its closing parenthesis.
c. Type a comma, the Monthly step, and the check query, so that the query reads as below. Run it.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.3: step 3, the two steps joined by month
   WITH MonthlyOutput AS (
       SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', pc.CompletionDate) AS Month,
           SUM(pcl.QuantityCompleted * i.StandardLaborHoursPerUnit)
               AS StandardHours
       FROM ProductionCompletionLine AS pcl
           INNER JOIN ProductionCompletion AS pc
               ON pc.ProductionCompletionID = pcl.ProductionCompletionID
           INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = pcl.ItemID
       WHERE pc.CompletionDate
           <= (SELECT MAX(WorkDate) FROM LaborTimeEntry)
       GROUP BY Month
   ),
   MonthlyHours AS (
       SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', WorkDate) AS Month,
           SUM(CASE LaborType WHEN 'Direct Manufacturing'
               THEN RegularHours + OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END)
               AS DirectHours,
           SUM(CASE LaborType WHEN 'Indirect Manufacturing'
               THEN RegularHours + OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END)
               AS IndirectHours,
           SUM(OvertimeHours) AS OvertimeHours
       FROM LaborTimeEntry
       WHERE LaborType <> 'NonManufacturing'
       GROUP BY Month
   ),
   Monthly AS (
       SELECT o.Month, o.StandardHours, h.DirectHours,
           h.IndirectHours, h.OvertimeHours
       FROM MonthlyOutput AS o
           INNER JOIN MonthlyHours AS h ON h.Month = o.Month
   )
   SELECT COUNT(*) AS Months FROM Monthly;
   ```

The query defines three steps and counts the rows of the third. It returns 36, the same as each step on its own, so every month found its match. A CTE can be run only together with the steps it uses, so each check repeats the steps before it, and the query is complete at every stage.

**Step 4. Add the trailing twelve months.** The fourth step calculates the monthly ratio and the trailing twelve-month figures over a named window, and the final SELECT keeps the months whose window holds twelve months.

a. Copy the query of Step 3, with its comment, to the end of the script, and change the comment to the one below.
b. Delete the last line, `SELECT COUNT(*) AS Months FROM Monthly;`, type a comma after the closing parenthesis of the Monthly step, and add the Trailing step and the final SELECT, so that the query reads as below. Run it.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.3: step 4, the trailing twelve months
   WITH MonthlyOutput AS (
       SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', pc.CompletionDate) AS Month,
           SUM(pcl.QuantityCompleted * i.StandardLaborHoursPerUnit)
               AS StandardHours
       FROM ProductionCompletionLine AS pcl
           INNER JOIN ProductionCompletion AS pc
               ON pc.ProductionCompletionID = pcl.ProductionCompletionID
           INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = pcl.ItemID
       WHERE pc.CompletionDate
           <= (SELECT MAX(WorkDate) FROM LaborTimeEntry)
       GROUP BY Month
   ),
   MonthlyHours AS (
       SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', WorkDate) AS Month,
           SUM(CASE LaborType WHEN 'Direct Manufacturing'
               THEN RegularHours + OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END)
               AS DirectHours,
           SUM(CASE LaborType WHEN 'Indirect Manufacturing'
               THEN RegularHours + OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END)
               AS IndirectHours,
           SUM(OvertimeHours) AS OvertimeHours
       FROM LaborTimeEntry
       WHERE LaborType <> 'NonManufacturing'
       GROUP BY Month
   ),
   Monthly AS (
       SELECT o.Month, o.StandardHours, h.DirectHours,
           h.IndirectHours, h.OvertimeHours
       FROM MonthlyOutput AS o
           INNER JOIN MonthlyHours AS h ON h.Month = o.Month
   ),
   Trailing AS (
       SELECT Month,
           ROUND((DirectHours + IndirectHours) / StandardHours, 2)
               AS HoursPerStandardHour,
           ROUND(SUM(DirectHours) OVER w
               / SUM(StandardHours) OVER w, 2) AS TTMDirect,
           ROUND(SUM(IndirectHours) OVER w
               / SUM(StandardHours) OVER w, 2) AS TTMIndirect,
           ROUND(SUM(DirectHours + IndirectHours) OVER w
               / SUM(StandardHours) OVER w, 2) AS TTMTotal,
           ROUND(SUM(OvertimeHours) OVER w
               / SUM(DirectHours + IndirectHours) OVER w, 3)
               AS TTMOvertimeShare,
           COUNT(*) OVER w AS MonthsInWindow
       FROM Monthly
       WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY Month
           ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
   )
   SELECT Month, HoursPerStandardHour, TTMDirect, TTMIndirect,
       TTMTotal, TTMOvertimeShare
   FROM Trailing
   WHERE MonthsInWindow = 12
   ORDER BY Month;
   ```

c. Read the TTMDirect, TTMIndirect, and TTMTotal columns from the first row to the last.
d. Read the TTMOvertimeShare column.

The WINDOW clause names the window, its order and its frame, once as w, and all nine window functions of the step use it. TTMDirect, TTMIndirect, and TTMTotal are the direct, indirect, and total hours per standard hour over the current month and the eleven before it, and MonthsInWindow counts the months in each window. The result starts in December 2024, the first month whose window holds twelve months. The monthly ratio jumps around, but the trailing figures tell a clear story. TTMIndirect climbs through the first half of fiscal 2025, as the months of 2024 with little indirect time leave the window, and then holds at a little over half an hour per standard hour. TTMDirect stays below one, but it creeps up through fiscal 2026. TTMTotal reaches its highest point in October 2026, and TTMOvertimeShare climbs in most months, from about a ninth of the hours to about a fifth. Each December's figures equal the ratios of Tutorial 10.3 for the year, because both count the labor time by the day worked and the output up to the same last day with time records.

**Step 5. Look at the months before the window is full.** The final SELECT keeps only the months whose window holds twelve months, and reversing the condition shows why.

a. In the query of Step 4, change `WHERE MonthsInWindow = 12` to `WHERE MonthsInWindow < 12`, and run the query.
b. Read the TTMTotal column of the first rows.
c. Change the condition back to `WHERE MonthsInWindow = 12`.

The query returns the months of 2024 before December, whose windows hold from one to eleven months. January 2024's window holds only the start-up month, when the plant recorded hours but completed almost nothing, and its figure is many times any other. The figures settle as the window fills, but they average fewer months than the rest, so keeping them would compare unlike periods. The full windows of December 2024 onward still include January 2024, which makes the first of them a little high.

**Step 6. Save the measure as a view.** A view stores the query under a name, and the name can then be queried like a table. The statements drop any earlier version of the view first, so that they can be run again whenever the query changes.

a. Copy the query of Step 4 to the end of the script, and change its comment to `-- Tutorial 11.3: the measure saved as a view`.
b. Delete the last line of the copy, `ORDER BY Month;`, and add a semicolon at the end of the line `WHERE MonthsInWindow = 12`.
c. Add the lines `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS MonthlyLaborEfficiency;` and `CREATE VIEW MonthlyLaborEfficiency AS` above `WITH`, so that the statements read as below.

   <!-- sql-check: view -->

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.3: the measure saved as a view
   DROP VIEW IF EXISTS MonthlyLaborEfficiency;
   CREATE VIEW MonthlyLaborEfficiency AS
   WITH MonthlyOutput AS (
       SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', pc.CompletionDate) AS Month,
           SUM(pcl.QuantityCompleted * i.StandardLaborHoursPerUnit)
               AS StandardHours
       FROM ProductionCompletionLine AS pcl
           INNER JOIN ProductionCompletion AS pc
               ON pc.ProductionCompletionID = pcl.ProductionCompletionID
           INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = pcl.ItemID
       WHERE pc.CompletionDate
           <= (SELECT MAX(WorkDate) FROM LaborTimeEntry)
       GROUP BY Month
   ),
   MonthlyHours AS (
       SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', WorkDate) AS Month,
           SUM(CASE LaborType WHEN 'Direct Manufacturing'
               THEN RegularHours + OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END)
               AS DirectHours,
           SUM(CASE LaborType WHEN 'Indirect Manufacturing'
               THEN RegularHours + OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END)
               AS IndirectHours,
           SUM(OvertimeHours) AS OvertimeHours
       FROM LaborTimeEntry
       WHERE LaborType <> 'NonManufacturing'
       GROUP BY Month
   ),
   Monthly AS (
       SELECT o.Month, o.StandardHours, h.DirectHours,
           h.IndirectHours, h.OvertimeHours
       FROM MonthlyOutput AS o
           INNER JOIN MonthlyHours AS h ON h.Month = o.Month
   ),
   Trailing AS (
       SELECT Month,
           ROUND((DirectHours + IndirectHours) / StandardHours, 2)
               AS HoursPerStandardHour,
           ROUND(SUM(DirectHours) OVER w
               / SUM(StandardHours) OVER w, 2) AS TTMDirect,
           ROUND(SUM(IndirectHours) OVER w
               / SUM(StandardHours) OVER w, 2) AS TTMIndirect,
           ROUND(SUM(DirectHours + IndirectHours) OVER w
               / SUM(StandardHours) OVER w, 2) AS TTMTotal,
           ROUND(SUM(OvertimeHours) OVER w
               / SUM(DirectHours + IndirectHours) OVER w, 3)
               AS TTMOvertimeShare,
           COUNT(*) OVER w AS MonthsInWindow
       FROM Monthly
       WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY Month
           ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
   )
   SELECT Month, HoursPerStandardHour, TTMDirect, TTMIndirect,
       TTMTotal, TTMOvertimeShare
   FROM Trailing
   WHERE MonthsInWindow = 12;
   ```

d. Select both statements and run them.

The message pane reports that execution finished without errors and that the query executed successfully, and no result grid appears, because the statements return no rows.

**Step 7. Find the view, and write it to the file.** The view exists in the open database at once, but it is saved in the file only when you write the changes.

a. On the **Database Structure** tab, find MonthlyLaborEfficiency under **Views**.
b. Click **Write Changes** on the toolbar, which the new view has made available, to save the view in CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite.

The view is now part of your working copy, as @fig-11-09 shows. It holds the query, not its result, so it will reflect any change in the data. Its six columns are the columns of the final SELECT, and it has no ORDER BY, because the order of the rows belongs to the query that uses it.

![The Saved View in the Database Structure Tab.](/visuals/svg/fig-11-09-view-in-structure.svg){#fig-11-09 fig-alt="A mock of the Database Structure tab of DB Browser for SQLite with CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite open. The Tables and Indices groups are collapsed with their counts. The Views group, with one view, is expanded and shows MonthlyLaborEfficiency with its six columns: Month, HoursPerStandardHour, TTMDirect, TTMIndirect, TTMTotal, and TTMOvertimeShare. The view is outlined, and the Triggers group below it is empty."}

**Step 8. Query the view.** The whole chain of steps now runs from one short query.

a. On the **Execute SQL** tab, type and run the query below at the end of the script.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.3: the view for fiscal 2026
   SELECT *
   FROM MonthlyLaborEfficiency
   WHERE Month >= '2026-01'
   ORDER BY Month;
   ```

b. Compare the result with the fiscal 2026 rows of Step 4.

The result, shown in @fig-11-10, holds the twelve months of fiscal 2026, with the same values as Step 4. The controller, or anyone else with the working copy, can run this query each month, after the new month's data arrives, and see at once whether the measure is still rising. Because the output stops at the last day with time records, the latest month is always compared over the days that its time records cover.

![The Monthly Measure for Fiscal 2026, Queried from the View.](/visuals/svg/fig-11-10-monthly-measure.svg){#fig-11-10 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL editor and its result. The editor, on the tab Chapter11.sql, is scrolled to a query that selects every column of the view MonthlyLaborEfficiency for the months from 2026-01 onward. The result grid shows twelve months with the monthly hours per standard hour, which swings from month to month, and the trailing twelve-month direct, indirect, and total hours per standard hour and overtime share, which change slowly. The trailing twelve-month columns are outlined."}

**Step 9. Complete and save the script.** The header comment should record the checks that the chapter's queries passed.

a. Replace the last line of the header comment of Chapter11.sql, so that the header reads as below.

   ```sql
   /* Chapter 11: the plant's hours, month by month
      Database: CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite (a copy of CharlesRiver.sqlite)
      Prepared by: your name, date
      Checks: the payroll ties to the ledger; the measure has 36 months */
   ```

b. Click **Save SQL file**.

The script now holds every query of the chapter under a comment that says what it answers, and a header that records the checks the results passed.

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- each step of the chain returns 36 months, including the join of the two summaries;
- the months before December 2024 have partial windows, led by the start-up month of January 2024;
- the trailing indirect hours per standard hour level off from the middle of fiscal 2025, while the trailing direct figure creeps up through fiscal 2026;
- the trailing total reaches its highest point in October 2026, and each December's figures equal the ratios of Tutorial 10.3;
- the view MonthlyLaborEfficiency appears under Views on the Database Structure tab of your working copy, and Write Changes has saved it;
- the query of the view for fiscal 2026 returns the same values as the full query;
- Chapter11.sql is saved with a completed header and a comment above each query.

The controller now has a measure that is smoothed enough to show a trend, split into the kinds of labor that explain it, and saved so that it runs again every month. Its parts point the same way: more time away from the work orders since the middle of 2024 for the same output, and more of the direct work paid at overtime rates.
